country.name: Indonesia
country.tagline: Bali's north-coast vineyards, eight degrees south of the equator, harvested several times a year.

stats.note: No OIV figure; a few wineries, centred on Bali.

country.overview:
Indonesia's wine is almost entirely Balinese. In 1994 Ida Bagus Rai Budarsa, whose family made traditional rice and palm drinks, founded Hatten Wines in Sanur and began buying grapes from growers around Singaraja on Bali's dry north coast, an area with a long history of table-grape growing. With no winter, vines there are pruned to produce two or three crops a year, so harvests can happen in almost any month.

Hatten's first wine was a rosé from Alphonse Lavallée (locally called Belgia), still its best-known wine, followed by whites from Muscat Saint-Vallier and the local Probolinggo Biru, and a traditional-method sparkling wine, Tunjung. Sababay Winery, founded in 2010 in Gianyar, works with cooperatives of northern farmers. Other Balinese brands use imported grape juice, so Indonesian labels are worth reading closely. Wine is made mostly for Bali's tourist trade; in a majority-Muslim country, alcohol taxes are very high.

history.title: Hatten Wines
history.text: Ida Bagus Rai Budarsa founded Hatten Wines, Indonesia's first modern winery, using grapes from Bali's north coast.

history.title: Sababay
history.text: Sababay Winery opened in Gianyar, sourcing grapes from cooperatives of north Bali farmers.

country.climate_soils: Tropical, with a dry season from about April to October on Bali's north coast, which lies in the rain shadow of the central volcanoes; volcanic soils near sea level.

grapes.name: Alphonse Lavallée (Belgia)
grapes.note: A black table grape used for rosé and red.

grapes.name: Muscat Saint-Vallier
grapes.note: A hybrid used for aromatic whites.

sites.name: Hatten Wines
sites.text: Bali's pioneering winery, founded in 1994 by Ida Bagus Rai Budarsa, with its winery and tasting room near Sanur. Its grapes come from growers around Singaraja on the north coast, where vines yield more than once a year; its Aga rosé and Tunjung sparkling are its best known wines.

sites.name: Singaraja vineyards (Buleleng)
sites.text: The dry north coast of Bali around Singaraja, in the rain shadow of the island's volcanoes, has grown table grapes for decades; it supplies Hatten and Sababay, and its vines can be cropped two or three times a year.
